title: Reading vision that faded over two months
stem: A 52-year-old man with type 2 diabetes of 18 years, HbA1c 9.8%, reports two months of blur in the right eye. BVA 20/60 OD, 20/25 OS. OD: flat new vessel fronds at the disc and on the superior arcade, faint vitreous haze, dot-blot haemorrhages in four quadrants, venous beading. OCT OD shows cystoid spaces through the fovea, central subfield 445 µm. IOP 16 both eyes, angles open, iris without vessels.

items.q: Which classification best fits the right eye?

options.t: Severe non-proliferative retinopathy with centre-involving oedema
Proliferative retinopathy with centre-involving macular oedema
Moderate non-proliferative retinopathy, oedema off the centre
Proliferative retinopathy with vitreous haemorrhage, no oedema
Ocular ischaemic syndrome on a background of retinopathy

items.why: Fronds at the disc and on the arcade are new vessels, which places the eye past non-proliferative disease. Cystoid thickening through the fovea at 445 µm makes the oedema centre-involving.

dis.label: Severe NPDR
dis.tempting: Haemorrhage in four quadrants and venous beading do meet the severe count.
dis.ruled: New vessels are present, and their presence alone ends the non-proliferative grade.

dis.label: PDR without oedema
dis.tempting: The fronds and the vitreous haze dominate, so the macula gets read second.
dis.ruled: Cystoid spaces through the fovea at 445 µm are oedema at the centre.

items.q: What is the most appropriate initial treatment of the right eye?

options.t: Panretinal photocoagulation at this visit, macular review in three months
Intravitreal anti-VEGF now, panretinal laser once the centre is drier
Focal macular laser to the leaking points, then panretinal laser
Dexamethasone implant now, with panretinal laser deferred six months
Vitrectomy with endolaser and anti-VEGF given at the end of surgery

items.why: Anti-VEGF answers both problems at once: new vessels regress and the fovea dries. Panretinal laser applied over a thick centre worsens acuity first, so it follows rather than leads.

dis.label: Panretinal laser first
dis.tempting: Laser is the definitive treatment for proliferation and this eye needs it.
dis.ruled: Scatter laser over centre-involving oedema drives thickness and acuity the wrong way.

dis.label: Vitrectomy
dis.tempting: Vitreous haze reads as bleeding, and surgery clears the media in one step.
dis.ruled: The haze is faint and the view supports laser and injection, so surgery waits.

items.q: Which three steps belong in the plan alongside intravitreal treatment?

options.t: Same-week diabetes team review of glycaemic control and blood pressure
OCT of both maculae at each treatment visit to guide retreatment
Dilated assessment of the left eye for proliferation and its own need
Stopping aspirin because the vitreous is already showing some blood
Deferring the next dilated examination for six months of injections
Advising that all reading be done with a stronger near addition

items.short: Systemic review, serial OCT, fellow eye
items.why: An HbA1c of 9.8% and an untreated fellow eye drive the eye disease as hard as any injection does. Retreatment is decided on measured thickness, so OCT is repeated at each visit.

dis.label: Stopping aspirin
dis.tempting: Antiplatelet therapy with blood in the vitreous feels like an obvious risk.
dis.ruled: Aspirin does not worsen diabetic haemorrhage, and stopping it costs cardiac cover.

dis.label: Six-month dilated review
dis.tempting: Monthly injection visits give the impression the eye is being watched.
dis.ruled: Injection visits do not examine the periphery, where proliferation progresses.

items.q: Which mechanism most directly explains the thickening at the fovea?

options.t: Breakdown of the inner blood-retinal barrier at capillary endothelium
Failure of the pigment epithelial pump at the outer blood-retinal barrier
Traction on the fovea by a taut thickened posterior hyaloid membrane
Loss of choriocapillaris perfusion beneath the central macula
Osmotic swelling of Muller cells driven by hyperglycaemia alone

items.why: Pericyte loss and damaged endothelial tight junctions let plasma into the retina, which collects in the outer plexiform and inner nuclear layers as the cystoid spaces seen here.

dis.label: Outer barrier pump failure
dis.tempting: The pigment epithelium does clear subretinal fluid, so its failure floods the macula.
dis.ruled: That mechanism gives serous elevation, not intraretinal cysts.

dis.label: Taut posterior hyaloid
dis.tempting: A real diabetic pattern, and traction genuinely thickens the fovea.
dis.ruled: No hyaloid deformation of the fovea is described, only cystoid spaces.

items.q: After three monthly injections the central subfield is 402 µm and acuity 20/60. What next?

options.t: Continue the same agent monthly for three further doses
Switch to a different anti-VEGF agent and reassess after three doses
Keep monthly injections and add a dexamethasone implant now
Stop injections and complete panretinal photocoagulation instead
Refer for vitrectomy with peeling of the internal limiting membrane

items.why: Thickness fell under 10% across a full loading course and acuity has not moved, which defines a poor response rather than a slow one. Changing agent is the next step before changing class.

dis.label: Same agent, three more
dis.tempting: Some eyes are slow responders, and persistence is often rewarded.
dis.ruled: A 43 µm fall over three doses is non-response, not slow response.

dis.label: Vitrectomy with peel
dis.tempting: Surgery is the recognised answer to oedema that will not dry.
dis.ruled: Peeling is for tractional oedema, and no traction is present here.

rules: If new vessels and centre-involving oedema sit together, dry the centre with anti-VEGF before laying panretinal laser. If thickness barely moves across loading, change the drug.

title: Vision clouded over in one eye on waking
stem: A 68-year-old man noticed painless blur in the left eye on waking three days ago. Treated hypertension, home readings 158/96. No diabetes. BVA 20/25 OD, 20/200 OS. Trace RAPD OS. IOP 15 both eyes, angles open, iris without vessels. OS: veins dilated and tortuous in four quadrants, flame and dot haemorrhages to the periphery, several cotton wool spots, blurred hyperaemic disc, central subfield 620 µm.

items.q: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.t: Undiagnosed severe non-proliferative diabetic retinopathy
Central retinal vein occlusion with macular oedema
Hemiretinal vein occlusion with macular oedema
Ocular ischaemic syndrome from carotid disease
Papilloedema with bilateral venous stasis

items.why: Haemorrhage and venous dilatation occupy all four quadrants of one eye, which places the obstruction at the central trunk. Unilateral disease with a normal fellow eye excludes the systemic patterns.

dis.label: Hemiretinal occlusion
dis.tempting: It produces the same signs and is easy to accept without mapping the quadrants.
dis.ruled: Hemiretinal disease respects the horizontal midline. All four quadrants are involved.

dis.label: Severe NPDR
dis.tempting: Dot haemorrhages and cotton wool spots are the diabetic vocabulary.
dis.ruled: Onset overnight in one eye only, and the fellow eye carries no retinopathy.

items.q: Which three findings raise the concern that this occlusion is ischaemic?

options.t: Relative afferent pupillary defect in the affected eye
Best corrected acuity of 20/200 in the affected eye
Several cotton wool spots at the posterior pole
Veins dilated and tortuous in all four quadrants
Central subfield thickness measured at 620 µm
Blurred disc margin with a hyperaemic disc

items.why: Perfusion is judged on afferent function and capillary closure, not on how much blood or fluid is visible. An RAPD, acuity at 20/200 and cotton wool spots each point at closure.

dis.label: Thickness 620 µm
dis.tempting: It is the most abnormal number on the page and it does explain the blur.
dis.ruled: Thickness measures leakage. A very thick macula can sit on a perfused bed.

dis.label: Tortuous veins, full disc
dis.tempting: Both look dramatic and both belong to the occlusion.
dis.ruled: Both appear in perfused occlusion as well, so neither separates the two.

items.q: What is the most appropriate management of the macular oedema?

options.t: Macular grid laser to the thickened area, review at three months
Intravitreal anti-VEGF now, with monthly acuity and OCT review
Observation for three months, since many occlusions settle alone
Intravitreal dexamethasone implant as the first-line agent
Oral acetazolamide with aspirin and review at six weeks

items.why: Anti-VEGF is first line for oedema after venous occlusion and it also suppresses the drive to anterior segment new vessels. Monthly review catches both non-response and rubeosis.

dis.label: Observation
dis.tempting: Spontaneous improvement is real, and the eye may recover without needles.
dis.ruled: Acuity is 20/200 with 620 µm of thickening. Waiting loses recoverable vision.

dis.label: Macular grid laser
dis.tempting: Grid laser is the older standard and it sounds definitive for leakage.
dis.ruled: Grid laser gave no acuity benefit in central occlusion and is not used for it.

items.q: Which systemic step matters most at this visit?

options.t: Same-week review of blood pressure and glucose in general practice
Carotid duplex within the week to exclude a stenosis on the affected side
Thrombophilia screen, given the inherited risk of thrombosis
Immediate stroke unit referral for antiplatelet loading today
Erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein today

items.why: Home readings of 158/96 name the modifiable driver, and undetected diabetes is the other. Treating them protects the fellow eye, which is the outcome that matters most here.

dis.label: Carotid duplex
dis.tempting: It is the right investigation when the retinal problem is arterial.
dis.ruled: Carotid disease causes arterial events, not venous thrombosis at the disc.

dis.label: Thrombophilia screen
dis.tempting: Thrombosis invites a clotting workup and it feels thorough.
dis.ruled: At 68 with hypertension the yield is negligible. Reserve it for young patients.

items.q: Where does the obstruction sit anatomically?

options.t: At an arteriovenous crossing under a stiffened arteriole, superotemporally
In the vein at the lamina cribrosa, sharing a sheath with the artery
In the superior ophthalmic vein behind the apex, draining intracranially
At the choriocapillaris, where venules collect into the vortex veins
In the short posterior ciliary vessels around the optic nerve head

items.why: Artery and vein cross the lamina cribrosa inside one adventitial sheath, so arteriolar stiffening compresses the vein there and the resulting turbulence seeds thrombus.

dis.label: Arteriovenous crossing
dis.tempting: It is the correct site for the branch occlusion the signs otherwise resemble.
dis.ruled: A crossing lesion drains one sector. Four quadrants means the central trunk.

dis.label: Superior ophthalmic vein
dis.tempting: It is the next vessel downstream, so obstruction there sounds plausible.
dis.ruled: Orbital venous obstruction gives proptosis and dilated lid veins, absent here.

rules: If haemorrhage and dilated veins cross all four quadrants, the lesion is at the lamina cribrosa. If acuity, pupil or cotton wool spots are bad, treat the eye as ischaemic and watch the angle.

rows: Gradual blur over weeks, with ache in some eyes
Dense, four quadrants, up to the disc
Sparse, mid-peripheral, few at the posterior pole
Markedly narrowed, spontaneous pulsation on gentle pressure
Often low, because ciliary perfusion has fallen
pair.decider: Sparse mid-peripheral haemorrhage with narrowed arteries and a soft eye points to carotid disease, which sends the patient for urgent vascular imaging rather than for injections alone.

title: Flashes on Friday, and spots ever since
stem: A 58-year-old woman, -5.50 D in both eyes, has four days of new floaters and arcs of light in the right eye, worse in dim rooms. No shadow in the field. BVA 20/20 both eyes, IOP 14. OD: pigment granules in the anterior vitreous, a Weiss ring, no cells, settled blood inferiorly. With indentation, a horseshoe tear at 11 o'clock with a vitreous strand on the flap, retina flat, no subretinal fluid. OS: inferotemporal lattice, no breaks.

items.q: Which feature carries the highest risk of progression to detachment?

options.t: Pigment granules dispersed in the anterior vitreous
A horseshoe tear with traction on its flap
Settled vitreous blood inferior to the break
Lattice degeneration in the inferotemporal fellow eye
Axial myopia of -5.50 D in both eyes

items.why: A flap tear held open by a vitreous strand keeps pulling with every eye movement, so fluid can enter continuously. That combination carries the highest conversion rate of any break.

dis.label: Fellow eye lattice
dis.tempting: Lattice is the best known predisposing lesion and it is genuinely present.
dis.ruled: Lattice without breaks in a symptom-free eye is low risk and needs no treatment.

dis.label: Pigment and blood
dis.tempting: Both are the classic markers that a break exists somewhere.
dis.ruled: They point to the tear. They do not measure the traction that opens it.

items.q: What is the most appropriate management of the right eye?

options.t: Laser retinopexy surrounding the tear within 24 hours
Cryotherapy to the tear and laser to the fellow lattice
Review in two weeks with a drawing of the periphery
Scleral buckle to relieve the traction on the flap
Vitrectomy with endolaser and a gas tamponade

items.why: A symptomatic flap tear with the retina still flat is sealed by surrounding retinopexy, which is quick, safe in clinic and highly effective. Delay is what turns the break into a detachment.

dis.label: Review in two weeks
dis.tempting: Vision is 20/20 with no field loss, so the eye looks stable enough to watch.
dis.ruled: Acuity stays normal until the fovea goes. Traction is active now.

dis.label: Vitrectomy with gas
dis.tempting: Surgery removes the traction itself rather than walling off the break.
dis.ruled: The retina is attached. Intraocular surgery adds risk that laser does not carry.

items.q: Which two symptoms after retinopexy require same-day return?

options.t: A shadow spreading from the periphery towards the centre
A sudden fresh increase in floaters with new flashes
Mild ache around the brow for two days after laser
Faint glare in bright sunlight lasting about a week
Slight morning blur that clears after some blinking

items.short: Spreading shadow, or new floaters and flashes
items.why: Retinopexy seals one break but does not stop the vitreous separating further. A spreading shadow means fluid under the retina, and a fresh shower of floaters means a new break.

dis.label: Brow ache
dis.tempting: Pain after any laser feels like the sign that something has gone wrong.
dis.ruled: Brief ache follows the contact lens and the burns. It carries no retinal meaning.

dis.label: Glare, morning blur
dis.tempting: Both are new visual symptoms in an eye that has just been treated.
dis.ruled: Neither maps to retinal separation. Both settle without any intervention.

items.q: Why do tears of this kind form where they do?

options.t: Vitreous collagen inserts firmly at the posterior vitreous base, and separation tears there
The internal limiting membrane is thinnest at the equator, so it splits first under traction
Pigment epithelial adhesion is weakest superiorly, so the retina lifts there first
Choroidal vessels tether the retina at the equator and resist vitreous movement
The subretinal space is widest at the equator, so fluid enters most easily there

items.short: Firm adhesion at the posterior vitreous base
items.why: Syneretic vitreous collapses forward and pulls hardest on its firmest attachment, the posterior margin of the vitreous base. Traction concentrated at that line tears full thickness retina.

dis.label: Thin limiting membrane
dis.tempting: Something must be weakest where the retina breaks, so thickness sounds right.
dis.ruled: Break site follows where vitreous is attached, not where retina is thin.

dis.label: Weak superior adhesion
dis.tempting: Superior tears really are commoner, so a superior weakness sounds plausible.
dis.ruled: Superior tears reflect gravity acting on the collapsing gel, not local adhesion.

items.q: What does the standard of care require of the practitioner at this visit?

options.t: A referral letter posted today, with review arranged in one month
Same-day documented referral, the break located, warning symptoms in writing
Advice to attend an emergency department if the vision changes
A dilated record made now, with the patient asked to telephone in a week
Referral held until the vitreous blood clears enough to grade the break

items.why: A symptomatic flap tear is treated within days, so the referral is made the same day. The record carries the location and the written symptoms that oblige the patient to return at once.

dis.label: Posted letter, one month
dis.tempting: It refers and it documents, which covers the two obvious duties.
dis.ruled: Postal timing does not match a break that can detach within days.

dis.label: Wait for the blood
dis.tempting: A clearer view would let the whole periphery be graded properly.
dis.ruled: The break is already seen and the retina is flat. Waiting only loses the window.

rules: If floaters and flashes are new, indent and search the whole periphery. If a flap tear is found with the retina still flat, seal it within a day rather than review it.

title: Everything went black in one eye at breakfast
stem: A 74-year-old man lost the vision of his right eye painlessly 90 minutes ago. No headache, no scalp tenderness, no pain on chewing. Atrial fibrillation, on no anticoagulant. Blood pressure 176/92, pulse irregular at 96. BVA hand movements OD, 20/25 OS. Dense RAPD OD. OD: pale oedematous posterior retina, a cherry red spot, segmented columns in the arterioles, no plaque at the disc. IOP 16 both eyes.

items.q: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.t: Non-arteritic central retinal artery occlusion
Ophthalmic artery occlusion with choroidal ischaemia
Arteritic retinal occlusion in giant cell arteritis
Ischaemic central retinal vein occlusion
Non-arteritic anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy

items.why: Sudden painless loss with a pale inner retina, a cherry red spot and segmented arteriolar flow is inner retinal infarction. Untreated fibrillation supplies the embolic source.

dis.label: Ophthalmic artery occlusion
dis.tempting: Hand movements vision is severe enough to suggest the whole supply has gone.
dis.ruled: A cherry red spot needs an intact choroid under the fovea, so the choroid is perfused.

dis.label: Arteritic occlusion
dis.tempting: At 74 the arteritic form must be excluded, and it changes treatment completely.
dis.ruled: No headache, scalp tenderness or jaw pain, and the embolic source is already known.

items.q: What is the most appropriate immediate action?

options.t: Ocular massage and paracentesis, with stroke referral tomorrow
Immediate transfer to a stroke unit for assessment and imaging
Carotid duplex in clinic today, cardiology review next week
High dose oral prednisolone now, pending inflammatory markers
Intravenous acetazolamide with rebreathing to raise carbon dioxide

items.short: Immediate transfer to a stroke unit
items.why: Retinal artery occlusion is an acute ischaemic stroke of the eye, and at 90 minutes the patient is inside the window where brain imaging and prevention change outcome.

dis.label: Massage, then refer
dis.tempting: These manoeuvres are the traditional bedside response and cost nothing to try.
dis.ruled: Neither has proven benefit, and the overnight delay wastes the stroke window.

dis.label: Duplex today, cardiology later
dis.tempting: It investigates the source and looks appropriately urgent.
dis.ruled: Investigation without a stroke pathway leaves the brain unprotected today.

items.q: Which three belong in the same-day workup?

options.t: Erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein today
Blood pressure, rhythm assessment and an electrocardiogram
Carotid imaging arranged within the coming week
Fluorescein angiography to time the arterial filling delay
Electroretinography to confirm inner retinal ischaemia
Thrombophilia screen before any anticoagulation is started

items.why: The workup asks where the embolus came from and whether arteritis is hiding. Markers, rhythm and carotid imaging answer that; the ocular tests only restate what the fundus already shows.

dis.label: Fluorescein angiography
dis.tempting: It documents the occlusion objectively and looks like the definitive test.
dis.ruled: The diagnosis is already clinical. Angiography delays the stroke referral.

dis.label: Thrombophilia screen
dis.tempting: It sounds like due diligence before committing to anticoagulation.
dis.ruled: At 74 with fibrillation the source is known, and the screen changes nothing.

items.q: Which new finding would move this towards an arteritic cause?

options.t: Scalp tenderness with pain in the jaw on chewing
Segmented columns of blood within the arterioles
A calcific plaque visible at the disc margin
Amaurosis fugax in the same eye last month
An irregular pulse at 96 with no anticoagulation

items.why: Arteritis is diagnosed on systemic features and markers, not on the fundus, because the retinal picture is identical. Jaw claudication is the most specific symptom in the set.

dis.label: Calcific plaque
dis.tempting: A visible plaque is dramatic and it proves the artery is diseased.
dis.ruled: A plaque names an embolic source, which argues against arteritis.

dis.label: Segmented columns
dis.tempting: It is the sign of stagnant arterial flow, which fits an inflamed vessel.
dis.ruled: Segmentation follows any severe occlusion, whatever closed the artery.

items.q: Which anatomic feature explains the cherry red spot?

options.t: The fovea is thin and takes its oxygen from the perfused choroid
A cilioretinal artery supplies the fovea in most eyes and spares it
Foveal pigment epithelium is denser, so it reads red against pale retina
Xanthophyll at the fovea absorbs light scattered by swollen retina
Ganglion cells crowd the foveal centre and tolerate ischaemia longer

items.short: Thin fovea over a perfused choroid
items.why: Infarcted inner retina turns opaque and pale, but the fovea has almost no inner retina and is nourished by the choroid, so the intact red choroidal bed shows through it.

dis.label: Cilioretinal artery
dis.tempting: A cilioretinal artery genuinely spares central vision when one is present.
dis.ruled: It exists in a minority of eyes and spares a wedge of retina, not the red spot.

dis.label: Ganglion cell tolerance
dis.tempting: Survival of the central retina would explain a normal looking centre.
dis.ruled: Ganglion cells are absent at the foveal centre and die fastest elsewhere.

rules: If retinal arterial occlusion is diagnosed inside the stroke window, the destination is the stroke unit, not the eye clinic. If systemic arteritic symptoms are present, treat before biopsy.

title: A grey smudge in the middle of the page
stem: A 41-year-old man reports six weeks of a central grey patch in the right eye, with objects on that side looking smaller and further away. He finished a course of oral corticosteroid for back pain three weeks ago and works night shifts. BVA 20/40 OD, improving to 20/30 with +1.00, 20/20 OS. OD: shallow serous elevation at the macula, no blood, no drusen, fine pigment flecks. OCT: subfoveal fluid, choroid 470 µm.

items.q: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.t: Pachychoroid neovasculopathy with a type 1 membrane
Acute central serous chorioretinopathy
Optic disc pit maculopathy with subretinal fluid
Inflammatory choroidal neovascular membrane
Cystoid macular oedema of uncertain cause

items.why: A shallow serous detachment with a thickened choroid, micropsia and a hyperopic shift in a man of 41 weeks after corticosteroid exposure is the classic presentation. No blood and no drusen.

dis.label: Pachychoroid neovascular
dis.tempting: It shares the thick choroid and the same age group, and it also leaks fluid.
dis.ruled: No subretinal hyper-reflective material and no haemorrhage on OCT or fundus.

dis.label: Cystoid macular oedema
dis.tempting: Central blur with distortion is the everyday description of macular oedema.
dis.ruled: The fluid is under the retina, not in cystoid spaces within it.

items.q: Which two features argue against a neovascular membrane?

options.t: Subretinal fluid with no hyper-reflective material
No drusen in either macula at the age of 41
Micropsia with distortion on the Amsler chart
A hyperopic shift of +1.00 in the affected eye
Choroidal thickness measured at 470 µm

items.why: A membrane shows as hyper-reflective tissue above the pigment epithelium, usually with blood, and usually on a drusen-bearing macula. Their absence is what argues against it.

dis.label: Thick choroid
dis.tempting: A thick choroid is the signature of serous disease, so it feels exclusive to it.
dis.ruled: Pachychoroid neovascular membranes grow on exactly this thick choroid.

dis.label: Micropsia, hyperopic shift
dis.tempting: Both are textbook symptoms of the serous condition being considered.
dis.ruled: Both follow from any fluid lifting the fovea, membrane or not.

items.q: What is the most appropriate management now?

options.t: Observation to three months, with steroid avoidance and sleep advice
Half-dose photodynamic therapy to the leaking area within two weeks
Intravitreal anti-VEGF monthly for three doses, then reassessment
Oral eplerenone for three months with electrolyte monitoring
Focal laser to the leakage point identified on angiography

items.short: Observe to three months, remove steroid
items.why: Most acute serous detachments resolve without treatment inside three months, and the recent corticosteroid course is a removable driver. Treatment is held for persistence or recurrence.

dis.label: Photodynamic therapy now
dis.tempting: It is the most effective treatment, so offering it early looks like good care.
dis.ruled: At six weeks the natural course is still resolution. Early treatment adds risk.

dis.label: Anti-VEGF
dis.tempting: Subretinal fluid at the macula is the situation anti-VEGF usually treats.
dis.ruled: Without new vessels there is no target, and trials show no benefit.

items.q: Four months on, fluid persists and acuity has fallen to 20/50. What next?

options.t: Half-dose photodynamic therapy guided by angiography
Continued observation for a further three months
Monthly intravitreal anti-VEGF for three doses
Oral eplerenone with two-weekly electrolytes
Full-fluence photodynamic therapy to the leak

items.why: Fluid past three to four months threatens the photoreceptors, and reduced-dose photodynamic therapy has the best evidence for resolving it while sparing the pigment epithelium.

dis.label: Observe three months more
dis.tempting: The condition is known for resolving on its own, so patience feels safe.
dis.ruled: Past four months the outer retina thins irreversibly. The window is closing.

dis.label: Full-fluence therapy
dis.tempting: It uses the right modality and full dose sounds more likely to work.
dis.ruled: Full fluence carries atrophy and ischaemia risk that the half dose avoids.

items.q: Which structure is the primary site of the disease?

options.t: Choroid, whose hyperpermeable vessels overwhelm the pigment epithelium
Retinal capillary endothelium, with inner barrier breakdown at the fovea
Bruch membrane, through defects of which new vessels grow forward
Outer plexiform layer, where Muller cells swell and form cysts
Vitreoretinal interface, where traction lifts the photoreceptors

items.why: Choroidal congestion and hyperpermeability drive fluid at the pigment epithelium faster than its pump can clear it, so fluid collects under the retina. The measured choroidal thickness is the clue.

dis.label: Inner barrier breakdown
dis.tempting: It is the mechanism behind most macular fluid a candidate sees.
dis.ruled: Inner barrier failure gives intraretinal cysts, not a smooth serous dome.

dis.label: Bruch membrane defects
dis.tempting: The pigment epithelium is involved, so its basement complex sounds central.
dis.ruled: That is the route for neovascular disease, which this eye does not show.

rules: If a young adult has serous macular fluid, look for steroid exposure and a thick choroid, and observe to three months. If fluid persists past four months, treat rather than watch.

rows: Usually past sixty, drusen in both maculae
Fluid with hyper-reflective tissue, thin choroid
Present in most eyes at some stage
pair.decider: Hyper-reflective material above the pigment epithelium, or any haemorrhage, means a membrane and same-week anti-VEGF. Its absence with a thick choroid buys three months of observation.

title: A drug the rheumatologist started five years ago
stem: A 46-year-old woman with systemic lupus erythematosus takes hydroxychloroquine 400 mg daily, started five years ago. Weight 61 kg, eGFR 88, no tamoxifen, no other ocular medication. Reading is unchanged. BVA 20/20 both eyes. Maculae show no pigment disturbance and no ring of depigmentation. Automated 10-2 fields are full, spectral domain OCT shows an intact outer retina, and no baseline record exists.

items.q: What does the current dose require of the practitioner?

options.t: Continue as prescribed, since retina, fields and acuity are normal
Report to the prescriber that the dose exceeds 5 mg/kg and needs review
Advise stopping the drug today, pending further macular imaging
Halve the dose in clinic now and repeat the fields in a year
Ask that the dose be recalculated on ideal rather than actual weight

items.why: At 61 kg, 400 mg daily is 6.6 mg/kg of actual body weight, above the 5 mg/kg threshold that raises retinopathy risk sharply. Dosing belongs to the prescriber, so the finding is reported with its reason.

dis.label: Continue as prescribed
dis.tempting: Every test today is normal, so there seems to be nothing to act on.
dis.ruled: Risk is set by cumulative dose. Normal screening now does not license the dose.

dis.label: Use ideal body weight
dis.tempting: Ideal weight dosing was the old rule and it is still widely quoted.
dis.ruled: Actual body weight replaced it, because it predicts toxicity better.

items.q: Which two tests form the core of annual screening here?

options.t: Spectral domain OCT of the macula
Automated 10-2 threshold visual fields
Fundus autofluorescence of the pole
Colour vision with pseudoisochromatic plates
Weekly Amsler chart testing at home

items.why: Screening pairs one structural and one functional test, because either can show the parafoveal change first. Autofluorescence and multifocal electroretinography are adjuncts, not the core.

dis.label: Autofluorescence
dis.tempting: It shows the parafoveal ring beautifully once damage is established.
dis.ruled: It is an adjunct, and it changes late compared with OCT and fields.

dis.label: Colour plates, Amsler
dis.tempting: Both are cheap, quick, and test central function of a sort.
dis.ruled: Neither is sensitive to parafoveal loss, which spares the very centre early.

items.q: Which pattern would indicate early toxicity?

options.t: Parafoveal outer retinal thinning with the foveal centre intact
Loss of the ellipsoid zone directly beneath the foveal centre
Cystoid spaces in the inner nuclear layer around the fovea
Drusenoid elevation of the pigment epithelium temporal to fixation
Choroidal thickening beneath the central macula on enhanced imaging

items.why: Toxicity starts two to six degrees from fixation, thinning the outer nuclear layer and ellipsoid zone in a ring while the centre stays normal. The fundus still looks unremarkable at that stage.

dis.label: Subfoveal ellipsoid loss
dis.tempting: The bull's eye name suggests the centre is the target of the damage.
dis.ruled: The centre is spared until late. Central loss points to another disease.

dis.label: Drusenoid elevation
dis.tempting: It sits parafoveally, which matches where toxicity is looked for.
dis.ruled: Drusenoid change is age-related deposition, not drug-related thinning.

items.q: Screening at year seven shows parafoveal ellipsoid loss and a 10-2 ring defect. What next?

options.t: Report to the prescriber this week so the drug can be withdrawn
Repeat the fields and OCT in six months before advising a change
Tell the patient to stop the drug today and inform the prescriber later
Advise halving the dose and continue annual screening as before
Add autofluorescence and electroretinography before any advice

items.why: Structure and function agree, which is definite toxicity, and damage continues after the drug stops. Withdrawal is the prescriber's decision and it is needed within days, not months.

dis.label: Patient stops it today
dis.tempting: It is fast and it puts the patient in control of her own risk.
dis.ruled: Abrupt withdrawal without the prescriber risks a lupus flare.

dis.label: Repeat in six months
dis.tempting: Confirming a screening finding before acting is usually good practice.
dis.ruled: Two agreeing tests already confirm it, and six months adds permanent loss.

items.q: What does the duty of care require of the screening record?

options.t: Annual results kept in the practice record and released only on written request
Baseline images and fields on file, with every result sent to the prescriber
A consent form for screening signed and filed before each annual visit
The prescriber's dose calculation copied into the record each year
A written note that continuing the drug is at the patient's own risk

items.short: Baseline on file, results to the prescriber
items.why: Screening detects change, which needs a documented starting point, and only the prescriber can act on the result. No baseline exists here, so establishing one is part of this visit.

dis.label: Kept, released on request
dis.tempting: Records are confidential, so waiting to be asked sounds correct.
dis.ruled: Shared care obliges active communication to the prescriber, not storage.

dis.label: Note of patient risk
dis.tempting: It documents that risk was discussed, which feels protective.
dis.ruled: It transfers a clinical duty to the patient. The duty is to inform the prescriber.

rules: If the daily dose exceeds 5 mg/kg of actual weight, report it whatever the retina looks like. If structure and function agree on parafoveal loss, that is toxicity and the drug must stop.

title: Pressures that crept up between two visits
stem: A 63-year-old woman has no visual symptoms. Her mother went blind from glaucoma. Asthma controlled on an inhaler, no other medication, resting pulse 54. BVA 20/20 both eyes. Goldmann IOP 26 OD, 28 OS. Central corneal thickness 545 and 548 µm. Gonioscopy: open to the ciliary band, no pigment band, no pseudoexfoliation. Cup-disc 0.75 OD and 0.8 OS with inferior rim thinning. Repeatable 24-2: superior nasal step OS, full OD.

items.q: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.t: Primary open angle glaucoma, worse in the left eye
Ocular hypertension with physiologically large cups
Normal tension glaucoma with asymmetric discs
Pigmentary glaucoma at an early stage
Secondary glaucoma from pseudoexfoliation

items.short: Primary open angle glaucoma, worse OS
items.why: Open angles, pressures in the mid twenties, inferior rim thinning and a matching superior nasal defect on repeatable fields complete the diagnosis. Gonioscopy excludes the secondary causes.

dis.label: Ocular hypertension
dis.tempting: Acuity is normal and she has no symptoms, so nothing seems lost yet.
dis.ruled: A repeatable nasal step with matching rim thinning is established damage.

dis.label: Normal tension glaucoma
dis.tempting: Asymmetric discs with a family history is the usual normal tension story.
dis.ruled: Pressures of 26 and 28 on normal corneas are not normal tension.

items.q: Which first-line topical agent fits this patient?

options.t: Timolol 0.5% twice daily in both eyes, with punctal occlusion taught
A prostaglandin analogue at night in both eyes
Brinzolamide 1% three times daily in both eyes
Brimonidine 0.2% twice daily in both eyes
Pilocarpine 2% four times daily in both eyes

items.why: A pulse of 54 with asthma rules out a beta-blocker whatever the drop technique. A prostaglandin gives the largest single-agent reduction on once nightly dosing, which also protects adherence.

dis.label: Timolol with occlusion
dis.tempting: Punctal occlusion is taught precisely to limit systemic absorption.
dis.ruled: It reduces but does not remove absorption. Asthma and bradycardia are absolute.

dis.label: Brinzolamide
dis.tempting: It avoids the respiratory and cardiac risk entirely, which looks safest.
dis.ruled: It lowers pressure less and dosing three times daily costs adherence.

items.q: Which three make up an adequate baseline before treatment starts?

options.t: Two repeatable threshold visual field examinations
Gonioscopy of both eyes with the angle graded
Central corneal thickness in both eyes
Anterior segment imaging used instead of gonioscopy
Corneal endothelial cell count in both eyes
Fundus autofluorescence of both maculae

items.why: Treatment is measured against a baseline, so the field must be repeatable, the angle mechanism must be known, and pressure must be interpreted against corneal thickness.

dis.label: Imaging over gonioscopy
dis.tempting: Angle imaging is objective, repeatable and comfortable for the patient.
dis.ruled: It cannot grade pigment, synechiae or recession, and it does not replace the lens.

dis.label: Cell count, autofluorescence
dis.tempting: Both are quantitative tests that fill out a thorough looking record.
dis.ruled: Neither informs glaucoma diagnosis, target setting or progression.

items.q: Three months on the prostaglandin, IOP is 21 OD and 23 OS. What next?

options.t: Continue the same drop and review again in six months
Add a topical carbonic anhydrase inhibitor and review in six weeks
Switch to the lowest available concentration of a beta-blocker
Refer for trabeculectomy in the left eye on the next available list
Repeat the visual fields before changing any treatment

items.short: Add a second agent, review at six weeks
items.why: A 25% reduction from 26 and 28 sets targets near 19 and 21, and the left eye with the field defect has not reached its. Adding a second agent is the next step, checked at six weeks.

dis.label: Continue, review later
dis.tempting: The pressure has fallen and a single drop is easier to sustain.
dis.ruled: The worse eye misses its target, and six months lets damage accumulate.

dis.label: Repeat fields first
dis.tempting: Progression is judged on fields, so more data before acting seems careful.
dis.ruled: Fields cannot change at twelve weeks. Pressure is the actionable number.

items.q: Which finding decides that this is glaucoma rather than ocular hypertension?

options.t: Inferior rim thinning matched by a nasal field defect
An intraocular pressure of 28 in the left eye by Goldmann
A cup-disc ratio of 0.8 in the left eye
A mother blinded by glaucoma in later life
Central corneal thickness of 548 µm

items.short: Rim thinning matched by a field defect
items.why: Ocular hypertension is raised pressure without damage. Structure and function agreeing in the same hemifield, the inferior rim and the superior field, is the damage that names the disease.

dis.label: Cup-disc 0.8
dis.tempting: A large cup is the image everyone associates with the diagnosis.
dis.ruled: Large discs carry large cups. Ratio alone cannot separate the two.

dis.label: Family history
dis.tempting: It raises risk severalfold and rightly changes how closely she is watched.
dis.ruled: Risk factors decide surveillance, not diagnosis.

rules: If the pulse is under 60 or the chest is asthmatic, no beta-blocker at any concentration. If structural loss and field loss agree in the same hemifield, treat it as glaucoma.

title: A red eye, a headache, and vomiting since evening
stem: A 66-year-old woman, +3.25 D in both eyes, has six hours of severe right brow ache with blurred vision and haloes around lights. She has vomited twice and took a cold remedy yesterday. BVA counting fingers OD, 20/25 OS. OD: injected conjunctiva, hazy oedematous cornea, mid-dilated oval unreactive pupil, very shallow chamber, IOP 54. No cells, no keratic precipitates, no lens opacity flecks. OS: IOP 18, narrow angle, no synechiae.

items.q: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.t: Acute primary angle closure with pupil block
Neovascular glaucoma with an angle membrane
Acute anterior uveitis with a raised pressure
Phacomorphic closure from an intumescent lens
Plateau iris syndrome after pharmacological dilation

items.why: A hyperopic eye with a very shallow chamber, a pressure of 54, corneal oedema and a fixed mid-dilated pupil is acute closure. The quiet chamber and clear lens exclude the secondary causes.

dis.label: Acute anterior uveitis
dis.tempting: Pain, redness and blurred vision are the uveitis triad, and pressure can rise.
dis.ruled: No cells and no keratic precipitates, and uveitis does not shallow the chamber.

dis.label: Plateau iris syndrome
dis.tempting: The cold remedy gives a dilating trigger, and plateau eyes close on dilation.
dis.ruled: Plateau eyes have a chamber of normal central depth and a flat iris plane.

items.q: What is the most appropriate immediate treatment?

options.t: Topical pressure lowering with oral acetazolamide, supine, review in an hour
Laser peripheral iridotomy at once, through the oedematous cornea, with no drops
Pilocarpine 2% now, repeated every five minutes for three doses
Intravenous mannitol as the first step, before any topical agent
Urgent lens extraction on the emergency list this evening

items.why: At 54 the iris sphincter is ischaemic and pilocarpine works poorly, and laser is unreliable through a hazy cornea. Lowering pressure medically clears the cornea and makes iridotomy possible.

dis.label: Intensive pilocarpine
dis.tempting: Constricting the pupil is the mechanism that should reopen the angle.
dis.ruled: A sphincter ischaemic at 54 will not respond, and repeated doses add anterior rotation.

dis.label: Immediate iridotomy
dis.tempting: Iridotomy is the definitive treatment, so doing it now sounds decisive.
dis.ruled: The oedematous cornea will not transmit the beam reliably or safely.

items.q: Which two steps belong in the definitive plan once the pressure falls?

options.t: Laser peripheral iridotomy to the affected eye
Prophylactic iridotomy to the fellow eye
Long-term prostaglandin drops in both eyes
Selective laser trabeculoplasty to the angle
Iridoplasty repeated at monthly intervals

items.why: Iridotomy removes the pressure gradient that bows the iris forward. The fellow eye is narrow with the same anatomy and roughly half of such eyes close within five years, so it is treated too.

dis.label: Long-term prostaglandin
dis.tempting: Drops lower pressure and feel like the standard glaucoma answer.
dis.ruled: Drops do not address the mechanism, and the angle can still close on them.

dis.label: Laser trabeculoplasty
dis.tempting: It is laser to the angle, which sounds like the right target.
dis.ruled: It needs a visible open angle to treat, and it does not relieve pupil block.

items.q: One week after iridotomy, IOP is 24 with synechiae over 20% of the angle. What next?

options.t: Start a topical pressure lowering agent and monitor the angle
Repeat the iridotomy at a second site in the same eye
Add pilocarpine long term to hold the angle open
Refer for trabeculectomy with an antimetabolite
Observe without treatment and review in three months

items.why: A patent iridotomy has relieved the block, so the residual pressure comes from synechial and trabecular damage. That is treated medically first, with gonioscopy to track any further closure.

dis.label: Second iridotomy
dis.tempting: If pressure remains high the first opening may look inadequate.
dis.ruled: A patent iridotomy needs no second site. The problem is now the angle itself.

dis.label: Observe three months
dis.tempting: The crisis has passed and 24 is far from the pressure she presented with.
dis.ruled: Synechiae progress silently, and this eye has already lost angle.

items.q: Which finding shows that pupil block, not a plateau configuration, drives the closure?

options.t: A convex iris with a very shallow central chamber in a hyperopic eye
A mid-dilated oval pupil that does not react to light
Corneal oedema at a pressure of 54 in that eye
A narrow angle in the fellow eye with no synechiae and normal pressure
Onset in the evening after a dose of cold remedy

items.why: Pupil block bows the whole iris forward and shallows the chamber centrally as well as peripherally. Plateau eyes keep a normal central depth with a flat iris and a forward ciliary body.

dis.label: Fixed mid-dilated pupil
dis.tempting: It is the signature sign of the attack and it is genuinely present.
dis.ruled: It reflects sphincter ischaemia at high pressure, whatever closed the angle.

dis.label: Cold remedy trigger
dis.tempting: A dilating drug precipitates both mechanisms, so it feels diagnostic.
dis.ruled: Plateau eyes close on dilation too. The trigger does not name the mechanism.

rules: If the cornea is oedematous at a very high pressure, lower the pressure medically before attempting laser. If one eye has closed, the fellow narrow eye gets a prophylactic iridotomy.

title: Ache and redness in the eye that failed in spring
stem: A 71-year-old man had an ischaemic central retinal vein occlusion in the right eye four months ago and now has three weeks of ache, redness and haloes. BVA counting fingers OD, 20/30 OS. OD: oedematous cornea, IOP 44, deep central chamber, fine vessels crossing the pupil margin onto the iris, gonioscopy shows fibrovascular tissue bridging the angle with synechiae over 180°. Disc pale, old haemorrhages. OS: IOP 15, angle open.

items.q: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.t: Neovascular glaucoma with a fibrovascular angle membrane
Acute angle closure in an eye with an old occlusion
Steroid response glaucoma after treatment of the occlusion
Ghost cell glaucoma from degenerate red blood cells
Uveitic glaucoma with trabeculitis and iris vessels

items.why: Ischaemic retina four months ago, new vessels at the pupil margin and fibrovascular tissue bridging the angle with broad synechiae is neovascular glaucoma at the synechial stage.

dis.label: Acute angle closure
dis.tempting: Ache, haloes, corneal oedema and a pressure of 44 read like an acute attack.
dis.ruled: The central chamber is deep, and the closure is by membrane over three weeks.

dis.label: Ghost cell glaucoma
dis.tempting: There has been intraocular blood, and degenerate cells do block outflow.
dis.ruled: Ghost cells need vitreous haemorrhage and give no iris or angle vessels.

items.q: Which two findings establish that the angle is closed by membrane, not apposition?

options.t: Fibrovascular tissue bridging the angle on gonioscopy
Peripheral anterior synechiae over 180° of the angle
Fine vessels crossing the pupil margin onto the iris
Corneal oedema at a pressure of 44 in that eye
Three weeks of increasing ache, redness and haloes

items.why: Appositional closure is reversible on indentation and leaves the angle anatomy intact. Tissue bridging the angle with permanent adhesions is mechanical closure that no drop can reopen.

dis.label: Vessels at pupil margin
dis.tempting: Rubeosis is the hallmark of the disease, so it feels like the answer.
dis.ruled: It proves neovascularisation, not that the angle is already sealed.

dis.label: Oedema, three weeks of ache
dis.tempting: Both show how high and how sustained the pressure has been.
dis.ruled: Neither examines the angle, and both occur with appositional closure.

items.q: What is the most appropriate management now?

options.t: Intravitreal anti-VEGF with topical pressure lowering, panretinal laser to follow
Panretinal photocoagulation alone now, with pressure drops and review in four weeks
Trabeculectomy with mitomycin C on the next available list
Cyclodiode laser now, with no retinal treatment planned
Retrobulbar alcohol for pain, since the eye sees very little

items.short: Anti-VEGF and drops, laser to follow
items.why: Anti-VEGF regresses the angle and iris vessels within days while drops carry the pressure, and panretinal laser then removes the ischaemic drive permanently. The order matters, not the choice.

dis.label: Panretinal laser alone
dis.tempting: It treats the underlying ischaemia, which is the root of the problem.
dis.ruled: It takes weeks to work and the cornea is too hazy to laser adequately now.

dis.label: Trabeculectomy
dis.tempting: Pressure is 44 with a sealed angle, which sounds like a drainage problem.
dis.ruled: Filtration fails in an actively neovascular eye. Regress the vessels first.

items.q: Pressure stays 38 on maximal drops, the eye is painful and sees hand movements. What next?

options.t: Cyclodiode laser to lower the pressure and settle the pain
Trabeculectomy with mitomycin C and a releasable suture
Glaucoma drainage device with a tube to the chamber
Enucleation, since the eye has no useful vision left
Retrobulbar chlorpromazine with the drops continued

items.short: Cyclodiode laser for pressure and pain
items.why: With minimal vision, a painful eye and a neovascular angle, reducing aqueous production is the lowest risk route to comfort. Filtering procedures scar closed and carry a real risk of loss.

dis.label: Drainage device
dis.tempting: Tubes are the recognised choice in neovascular glaucoma with vision.
dis.ruled: Reserved for eyes with useful vision. This eye needs comfort, not a tube.

dis.label: Enucleation
dis.tempting: It is definitive for a blind painful eye and ends the problem.
dis.ruled: Pain has not yet been treated. Enucleation is a last resort, not a next step.

items.q: Which mediator most directly drives the angle change?

options.t: Vascular endothelial growth factor from ischaemic retina
Prostaglandin released from a chronically inflamed uvea
Transforming growth factor beta from lens epithelium
Complement activated on the trabecular endothelium
Ferritin deposited from degraded intraocular blood

items.why: Hypoxic retina secretes vascular endothelial growth factor, which diffuses forward into the aqueous and drives new vessels on the iris and in the angle. That pathway is why anti-VEGF works within days.

dis.label: Uveal prostaglandin
dis.tempting: The eye is red and aching, so an inflammatory mediator fits the picture.
dis.ruled: Prostaglandins cause inflammation and lower pressure. They grow no vessels.

dis.label: Ferritin from old blood
dis.tempting: There was retinal haemorrhage, so iron products are genuinely present.
dis.ruled: Iron toxicity is a late siderotic process and grows no fibrovascular tissue.

rules: If an ischaemic eye develops a high pressure with iris vessels, treat the ischaemia and the pressure together. If the eye is painful with no useful vision, cyclodestruction before filtration.

rows: Days to weeks of increasing ache
Hours, severe, with nausea and vomiting
Vessels at the pupil margin, membrane in the angle
No vessels, angle closed by apposition
pair.decider: A deep central chamber with vessels at the pupil margin means the closure is neovascular, so the treatment is anti-VEGF and retinal laser rather than iridotomy to either eye.

title: Ache behind the eye, then the colours went flat
stem: A 29-year-old woman has four days of worsening blur in the left eye with ache on eye movement, and says colours look washed out on that side. No headache. Two years ago she had a fortnight of numbness in the right leg that resolved without investigation. BVA 20/20 OD, 20/80 OS. RAPD OS. Ishihara 14 of 14 OD, 4 of 14 OS. Central depression on 24-2 OS. Both discs flat and normal in colour. IOP 14 both eyes.

items.q: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.t: Demyelinating retrobulbar optic neuritis
Non-arteritic anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy
Compressive optic neuropathy at the orbital apex
Leber hereditary optic neuropathy, first eye
Posterior ischaemic optic neuropathy after hypotension

items.why: A young woman with subacute unilateral loss, pain on movement, dyschromatopsia, an RAPD and a normal disc has retrobulbar inflammation. The earlier leg symptom points to demyelination.

dis.label: Anterior ischaemic
dis.tempting: It is the commonest optic neuropathy and shares the RAPD and colour loss.
dis.ruled: It needs a swollen disc and it does not hurt on eye movement.

dis.label: Apical compression
dis.tempting: Compression also spares the disc early and causes progressive loss.
dis.ruled: Compression progresses over months, without pain on movement.

items.q: Which feature best separates this from an ischaemic optic neuropathy?

options.t: Pain on eye movement with a normal disc at 29
A relative afferent pupillary defect on that side
Acuity of 20/80 with a central field depression
Four of fourteen Ishihara plates read correctly
An intraocular pressure of 14 in both eyes

items.short: Pain on movement with a normal disc
items.why: An RAPD, reduced acuity and dyschromatopsia occur in both, so neither separates them. Pain on movement with a flat disc in a woman of 29 is specific to inflammation of the nerve behind the globe.

dis.label: Afferent pupil defect
dis.tempting: It is the sign that proves the nerve is at fault, so it feels decisive.
dis.ruled: Any unilateral optic neuropathy gives it. It localises without discriminating.

dis.label: Ishihara 4 of 14
dis.tempting: Colour loss is taught as the marker of optic neuritis.
dis.ruled: Ischaemic neuropathy desaturates colour in proportion to acuity too.

items.q: What is the most appropriate management?

options.t: Contrast MRI of brain and orbits, with neurology referral
Intravenous methylprednisolone started today, imaging later
Oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg for eleven days with a taper
Observation alone, since most eyes recover their acuity
Same-day inflammatory markers and a temporal artery biopsy

items.why: Imaging counts the lesions that set the risk of multiple sclerosis and excludes compression, and that result drives disease modifying treatment. Steroids do not change the final acuity.

dis.label: Steroids first
dis.tempting: Treating the inflammation immediately feels like the active choice.
dis.ruled: Steroids only shorten the attack, and imaging must come before immunotherapy.

dis.label: Oral prednisolone
dis.tempting: It avoids admission and appears to give the same anti-inflammatory effect.
dis.ruled: Standard oral dosing alone was associated with more recurrent attacks.

items.q: Which two statements belong in the counselling?

options.t: Most eyes recover useful acuity over two to three months
Steroids speed recovery but do not change the final acuity
Low dose oral steroid prevents a second attack later
Colour vision returns fully in every case by six weeks
Recovery is unlikely once acuity has fallen to 20/80

items.short: Recovery expected, steroids only speed it
items.why: The natural history is good, with most eyes back near normal acuity within three months, and steroid benefit is confined to the speed of that recovery. Residual colour and contrast loss is common.

dis.label: Colour fully recovers
dis.tempting: Acuity recovers so well that colour is assumed to follow it.
dis.ruled: Colour and contrast deficits persist in many eyes with 20/20 acuity.

dis.label: Poor acuity, poor outcome
dis.tempting: Presenting acuity predicts outcome in most other optic neuropathies.
dis.ruled: Even eyes at counting fingers usually recover substantially here.

items.q: Which mechanism explains the ache on eye movement?

options.t: Traction on the inflamed nerve sheath by the muscle origins
Ischaemia of the short posterior ciliary arteries at the disc
Stretch of the ciliary nerves crossing the posterior sclera
Raised orbital pressure from oedema within the muscle cone
Meningeal irritation transmitted along the optic canal

items.short: Traction on the inflamed nerve sheath
items.why: The superior and medial rectus origins share the dural sheath of the nerve at the apex, so every movement pulls on an inflamed, swollen sheath. This is why the pain is worse on adduction and elevation.

dis.label: Ciliary artery ischaemia
dis.tempting: It is the mechanism of the disease this case must be separated from.
dis.ruled: Ischaemic neuropathy is painless, and the disc here is flat and normal.

dis.label: Raised orbital pressure
dis.tempting: Orbital congestion genuinely causes ache worsened by movement.
dis.ruled: There is no proptosis, no chemosis and no restriction of movement.

rules: If a young adult loses vision in one eye with pain on movement and a normal disc, image the brain and orbits before reaching for steroids. If the disc is swollen instead, rethink the diagnosis.

rows: Twenties to forties, worse over days
Past fifty, noticed on waking, then static
Ache on eye movement in most cases
Swollen, often segmental, with splinter haemorrhage
pair.decider: A swollen disc with an altitudinal field in an older patient moves the work to vascular risk and the fellow eye. A flat disc with pain on movement sends the patient for MRI and neurology.
